Building platforms

Site cut and levelling, to the level the design needs

Cut and fill, benching and building platform preparation. Taking a sloping or uneven block and leaving a platform at the level your engineer specified, compacted where that is in scope, with the material balanced on site where it can be and carted where it cannot. Send the engineering levels, and we will price the cut, the fill and the compaction.

0456 220 552

Carried out under demolition licence AD214737

Before anything starts

Six things have to be settled first, and not all of them are ours

Most jobs that run late run late on this list rather than on the work itself. Each line says who owns it.

  1. 01

    Levels and design platform

    Who You, through your surveyor or engineer

    The level we cut to comes from the design. Without it there is nothing to cut to.

  2. 02

    Cut and fill balance

    Who You, with your engineer

    Whether the material taken from the high side can be used on the low side, which decides how much leaves and how much is imported.

  3. 03

    Fill suitability

    Who You, through your consultant where it matters

    Not all excavated material is suitable as engineered fill. Which is which is a geotechnical question.

  4. 04

    Compaction requirement

    Who You, through your engineer

    What density, in what layer thickness, and who tests it.

  5. 05

    Retaining design

    Who You, through your engineer

    A cut that creates a face usually needs retaining, designed by others before the cut is made.

  6. 06

    Service location

    Who Max, with a locator

    Before anything goes in the ground.

The detail

Why a site cut is more than pushing dirt around

  • The level comes from the design. Not from what looks right. Cutting to the wrong level is a mistake that gets concreted over.
  • Fill has to be placed, not tipped. Material pushed into a low spot and left is where a slab finds a soft area two years later. Engineered fill goes in layers and is compacted.
  • Not everything excavated is suitable to reuse. Topsoil, organic material and some clays are not engineered fill, whatever they look like.
  • A cut face usually needs holding. Which is engineering work by others, and it has to be designed before the cut rather than after it.
  • The balance decides the cartage. A site that balances carts almost nothing. One that does not carts in both directions.
  • Rock changes the method mid cut. Particularly on the coastal side of Sydney, where a shelf can appear partway through.

Before you book

What people ask about this one

What level do you cut to?
The one on the drawings. We will not nominate it for you: that is your engineer’s call and the consequences of getting it wrong are structural rather than cosmetic.
Can the material from the cut be used as fill?
Sometimes. Topsoil and organic material cannot. Some clays are unsuitable as engineered fill. If it matters structurally, your geotechnical consultant answers it rather than us.
Do you compact it?
Where it is in scope, yes, in layers rather than one pass. Testing the result is geotechnical work and is done by your consultant, deliberately not by the contractor who placed it.
What about the cut face?
If it needs retaining, that is engineered and built by others, and it has to be designed before the cut is made rather than worked out afterwards.
How do I know if my block balances?
Your engineer calculates it from the levels and the design platform. It is worth knowing early, because a site that does not balance carries cartage in both directions.

Send the levels and the design platform

Levels and the platform level from your engineer. A site cut quoted without them is a guess about how much material moves.
